description: Draugar are the undead revenants of Icelandic saga and folklore, animated corpses that rise from graves and burial mounds. Corporeal and supernaturally strong, they swell to a huge size, bring disease and death to nearby farms, and can be fought but not easily killed. The best-known are Glámr in Grettis Saga and the mound-dweller Kárr the Old.
source: Grettis Saga; Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason
research_notes: Description was copy-pasted Drakos text; restored actual Draugar lore.

description: Draugen is the sea-revenant of Danish and Norwegian coastal folklore, the ghost of a fisherman or sailor drowned at sea. He appears as a drenched figure rising half from the water, sometimes rowing a half-boat, and his appearance or cry foretells drowning and shipwreck. Belief was strongest in Norwegian fishing communities, where the draug warned of storms.
source: Nordic maritime folklore; Scandinavian ethnographic collections
research_notes: Description was copy-pasted Draugar text; wrote correct Danish/Norwegian sea-ghost lore.

description: Along Sweden's Baltic coast and archipelagoes, the draugr is the revenant of a fisherman or sailor lost at sea. This maritime variant guards sunken treasure, raises storms, and harries living boatmen, reflecting the sea as both livelihood and grave. It is distinct from the mound-dwelling draugar of the Icelandic sagas.
research_notes: Entry misfiled under Iceland; corrected to the Swedish coastal tradition and removed template filler.

description: Eloko are forest spirits of the Mongo-Nkundo people of the Congo Basin, believed to be restless dead of ancestors who died with grudges. Fiercely territorial, they guard game and forest resources and are said to cast spells with enchanted bells that paralyze victims before they attack. They warn against neglecting ancestors and plundering the rainforest without respect.
research_notes: Removed template filler; content verified against Mongo-Nkundo tradition.

description: Mokele-Mbembe is a great water creature of Central African oral tradition, described by Bantu and Ba'Aka peoples as a large, long-necked, reptilian beast that lurks in deep river pools and swamps of the Congo Basin. Local reports later drew dozens of cryptozoological expeditions; science usually explains sightings as misidentified elephants, rhinos, or large snakes.
source: Bantu/Lingala oral tradition and cryptozoological literature
research_notes: Removed template filler; kept attested cryptid lore.

description: The Drekavac ('screamer') of South Slavic belief is the restless spirit of an unbaptized child that wails horribly at night, blending animal cries with human sobs. In parts of Bosnia it appears as a dappled, spindle-thin being or a spectral soldier, and its scream is said to foretell death or cattle disease. It shows itself at night, especially during the twelve 'unbaptized days' of Christmas.
source: South Slavic oral tradition; regional Bosnian collections
research_notes: Removed template filler.

description: Dreq, from Latin draco, is a dragon-demon of Albanian folk belief that rises from lakes and freshwater to attack livestock and people. Closely related to the multi-headed kulshedra, it takes a more draconic, vampiric form. Albanian tradition ties the dreq to dangerous waters, explaining drownings and mysterious deaths near lakes and rivers.
research_notes: Condensed; removed generic drowning/livestock padding.

description: In Belize the duende is Tata Duende (Nukuch Tat to the Yucatec Maya), a small forest guardian with backward-turned feet and no thumbs who whistles to lure or punish the unwary and protects animals and the bush. Parents warn children against the forest, for Tata Duende is said to steal the thumbs of careless children. He is a well-known figure of Belizean Maya and Creole folklore.
source: Belizean Maya and Creole oral tradition
research_notes: Corrected copy-pasted Peruvian text; Belize figure is Tata Duende/Nukuch Tat, featured on a Belize postage stamp.

description: El Duende of Ecuadorian folklore is a small forest spirit, a wrinkled little man in a broad hat and pointed shoes who guards forests and highlands while playing tricks, stealing food, and leading animals astray. He is said to lure disobedient children into the woods, where offending him can make one lose one's way forever, and he collects children's nail clippings as a protective charm.
research_notes: Corrected copy-pasted Peruvian text; wrote attested Ecuadorian duende belief.

description: Peruvian duende belief blends Quechua and Aymara tradition with Spanish colonial influence. In the Amazon the duende is close to the chullachaqui, a shapeshifting jungle spirit that guards the forest and misleads hunters; in the highlands it takes on mountain-spirit traits, watching over fields and communities. Parents use the figure to keep children from wandering alone in the bush.
source: Peruvian oral tradition; Quechua/Aymara ethnographic records
research_notes: Condensed; removed generic stewardship moralizing and template opener.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Duizendpoot is simply the modern Dutch word for a centipede (literally 'thousand-foot') and names no mythological being in Dutch tradition, where the nearest domestic or forest spirits are the kabouter and the klabauterman. The present description is a copy-pasted Belize duende text.
research_notes: Copy-pasted Belize duende text; Dutch duizendpoot means centipede, not a folklore being.

description: Duppy is the Bahamian term, shared across the English-speaking Caribbean, for the spirit of a dead person. Duppies are usually malevolent and wander at night, haunting the places they knew in life, and obeah practitioners may summon them or set them on others. Bahamians take precautions against duppies, reflecting an African-descended view of the dead lingering among the living.
research_notes: Corrected copy-pasted Kittitian text; duppy is attested in Bahamian usage.

description: Duppy is the Kittitian word for a restless ghost, from the Akan-derived vocabulary of the African diaspora. Duppies linger where they lived, especially plantations and lonely places, making noises, moving objects, and playing tricks, and can be vengeful if wronged in life. Kittitians avoid shouting a name at night lest a duppy answer, and the tall Mocko Jumbie stilt-walker wards them off.
source: St. Kitts and Nevis oral tradition
research_notes: Removed template filler.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Norwegian water-spirit named 'eintal' appears in folklore collections, and the proposed ein plus tal ('lone song') etymology is invented. The genuine lake-dwelling musician who enchants listeners with fiddle music is the nokken, and Telemark accounts of such a being belong to that figure.
research_notes: Fabricated Telemark nokken variant; closest genuine figure is the nokken.

description: El Silbon, the Whistler, is a specter of the Venezuelan llanos. A tall figure in white carrying his murdered father's bones in a sack, he whistles a tune that, if it sounds close, means he is far away and vice versa. Cursed by his grandfather for parricide, he stalks drunkards and womanizers and can be warded off by barking dogs, chili peppers, or a whip.
research_notes: Fixed mislocation to Mexico and removed 'snip' artifact; Silbon is Venezuelan/Colombian llanos folklore.

description: El Silbon, the Whistler, is a specter of the Venezuelan and Colombian llanos, wrongly placed here in Mexico. A tall man in white carrying his father's bones, he whistles in a way that deceives about his distance, preys on drunkards and womanizers, and is repelled by dogs, chili peppers, or a whip. The legend warns against parricide, family violence, and night wanderings.
research_notes: Duplicate of the Venezuela entry; Silbon is not Mexican folklore, corrected provenance.

description: Eototo is the chief of the Hopi katsinam, the spiritual counterpart of the Hopi village chief and 'father' of all katsinam. He knows all the ceremonies and appears at the Powamu ceremony in February, when he draws cloud symbols in cornmeal and pours sacred water into the kiva to bring rain for Hopi agriculture. Shabby in appearance, his power is not to be judged by looks.
research_notes: Removed invented Ometeotl (Aztec) derivation; Eototo is a real Hopi katsina chief.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Farsakh is a Persianate unit of distance (the parasang, roughly five to six kilometers), not a Pamiri giant, and the 'giant builder of terraces and fortresses' account is fabricated. The genuine giants of Iranian-influenced Central Asian tradition are the divs of Persian mythology.
research_notes: Name is a Persian distance unit (parasang); no giant figure exists.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No 'Fire Keeper' spirit appears in recorded Charrua tradition; the account is a modern AI-style retelling of an unwritten 'gratitude to fire' lesson. Surviving records of Charrua belief are sparse, and no named fire spirit is documented for them.
research_notes: Charrua 'Fire Keeper' traced to AI content farms; no genuine tradition.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Fjeldvig is a Norwegian place-name and surname, not a Danish folklore being, and the description grafts generic bjergfolk (hill-folk) lore onto the name. Genuine Danish mound-folk belong to the bjergfolk complex related to the nisse and trold; no being called Fjeldvig is recorded.
research_notes: Norwegian farm/surname; content is generic bjergfolk lore.

description: The Forest Person of Pacific Northwest tradition is Kushtaka (Kooshdaa kaa), the 'land otter man' of the Tlingit and neighboring peoples whose range extends from southeast Alaska into Canada. A shapeshifter straddling human and animal, it is tied to drowning: Kushtaka may rescue or transform the souls of the drowned. Similar beings appear among the Tsimshian and Dena'ina.
research_notes: Removed template filler; Kushtaka lore is real.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No sacred fox ancestor-spirit occurs in Aztec religion; the description conflates the fox with coyote figures such as Huehuecoyotl, the aged coyote trickster god, and invents messenger and calendar associations. The fox is not a significant figure in recorded Mexica mythology.
research_notes: AI content-farm claims; genuine analogue is Huehuecoyotl (coyote god).

description: In Lakota tradition the fox (sungila) is a notable animal in medicine and storytelling, and the Kit Fox Society (sungila okolakiciye) was a warrior order that policed the home camp and supplied food. The fox appears in tales as a clever figure valued for sharp wits and survival in dangerous country.
research_notes: Condensed; kept attested Kit Fox Society lore, dropped generic moralizing.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named Passamaquoddy fox ancestor-spirit or 'protective fox tracks' appears in Wabanaki collections; the description is generic woodland moralizing. The central culture hero of Passamaquoddy tradition is Gluskabe, and no developed fox spirit figure is documented.
research_notes: Generic Wabanaki fox moralizing; no named tradition.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox figure appears in Akan anansesem (spider-story) tradition, whose trickster is Ananse, and the hunting-omen claims are invented. The fox does not hold a developed role in recorded Ashanti animal tales.
research_notes: No Akan fox figure in anansesem tradition.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named Baloch fox spirit or fox trickster tale is recorded; the description is generic desert-animal moralizing. Genuine Baloch folklore preserves named tales and characters, but no attested fox tradition supports this entry.
research_notes: Generic fox-cunning content; no named Baloch tale.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox spirit or omen belief is recorded in Kikuyu oral collections, and the claimed meaning for the fox in Ngai's cosmos is invented. Kikuyu animal tales center on other creatures; no developed fox figure is documented.
research_notes: Invented omen claims; no named Kikuyu fox tradition.

description: In Cree oral tradition the fox appears as a shrewd, adaptable figure of the northern forests and plains, admired by hunters for thriving in harsh winters. Beyond general respect for the animal's cleverness, no named Cree fox deity is documented; the fox's role is that of a wise animal in tales rather than a formal spirit.
research_notes: Kept attested general belief; the fox is a tale figure, not a named deity.

description: The fox (chomak in Yucatec Maya) appears in Maya folk tales as a clever, cunning figure who outwits larger animals, and some accounts link the fox to night and trickster themes. Beyond general folk-tale use, no formal Maya fox deity is recorded in the codices or Popol Vuh.
research_notes: Removed invented omen/calendrical claims; chomak fox is a folk-tale figure.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Apache fire-stealing culture hero is Coyote, not a fox; the 'Fox Giant' is an invented conflation, and no such being appears in recorded Apache creation stories.
research_notes: Fire-thief is Coyote; Fox Giant is a fabricated conflation.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox giant exists in Aztec (Mexica) myth; the text itself conflates the fox with the tlacuache (opossum) and invents Tezcatlipoca associations and underworld-guide roles. These claims trace to AI content farms, not to Mesoamerican sources.
research_notes: Conflates fox with tlacuache; invented Tezcatlipoca links.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox spirit acts as messenger of Asase Yaa or keeper of sacred groves in Akan belief; those claims are invented. The Akan spirit world centers on figures such as Asase Yaa, Nyame, and the trickster Ananse, with no attested fox spirit.
research_notes: 'Asase Yaa messenger' and sacred-grove claims invented.

description: The Maya fox (chomak/ch'amak) is a folk-tale figure of cunning and transformation, and contemporary Maya communities tell stories of the clever fox. Claims that the fox aided the Hero Twins in the Popol Vuh or guarded sacred fire are not supported by the text; the fox is best attested as an everyday trickster of oral tradition.
research_notes: Removed invented Popol Vuh/Hero Twins connections.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox messenger or divination figure appears in recorded Muisca mythology; the claimed role as messenger of Sue and Chia and the links to Lake Guatavita and El Dorado are invented. Muisca tradition preserves no named fox spirit.
research_notes: Invented Sue/Chia and Guatavita links; no Muisca fox figure.

description: In Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition, the fox is one of the animal clan figures (doodem), representing cleverness and diplomacy, and appears in storytelling as a shrewd helper or trickster. Animal powers are respected in Anishinaabe medicine practice, and the fox is a real but minor spirit figure rather than a named deity.
source: Anishinaabe oral tradition; Great Lakes ethnography
research_notes: Removed template filler.

description: In Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition of the Great Lakes, the fox is a clan animal (doodem) linked to cleverness and diplomacy and appears in tales as a shrewd trickster. The fox is a respected minor spirit figure in medicine practice, not a formal deity; no dedicated fox deity is documented.
source: Anishinaabe oral tradition; Great Lakes ethnography
research_notes: Deduplicated from Canada entry; condensed.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Gaidhri' is a Gaelic-looking name with no attested Newari or Nepali tradition; the description is fabricated. The genuine Nepalese spirit of this household-forest type is the Newari Khyah, a large hairy household guardian.
research_notes: Name is Gaelic in character; real Newari figure is Khyah.

description: A goblin is a small, grotesque, mischievous spirit of English folklore, from the family of household and wilderness spirits that includes hobgoblins and boggarts. Goblins are chiefly pranksters who cause annoyance rather than real harm. The word likely comes from the French gobelin or medieval Latin gobelinus, and the figure has spread widely through literature and fantasy.
research_notes: Condensed; removed repetition ('hobgoblins, hobgoblins') and padding.

description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as a Danish being. The description is the English goblin entry copy-pasted with a filler line; 'goblin' names no Danish tradition, whose household spirit is the nisse and whose wilderness beings are the trold and elverfolk.
research_notes: English copy-paste; Danish equivalent is the nisse.
